name: Biacromial / clavicle width

card.summary: The bone-based width of the shoulder girdle, which looksmaxxers treat as a fixed frame limit that muscle can only add to.
card.aka: bone-set shoulder width, clavicle length, biacromial breadth
card.note: Mostly a measurement concept; no studies found on appearance effects.

quick.overview:
Biacromial width is the distance between the outer points of the shoulder blades, and clavicle length is the length of the collarbones. Looksmaxxers treat both as the skeletal limit on how wide the shoulders can look.

Community threads ask what counts as a good clavicle or bideltoid width and compare measurements, often in inches and at a stated height.
quick.mechanism: The clavicle is a horizontal strut between the sternum and shoulder blade. Males usually have longer clavicles than females, and the bone finishes ossifying around age 21 to 25. Muscle such as the deltoids sits on top of this frame and adds soft-tissue width.
quick.risks: Measuring is harmless, though community comparison can feed body-image concern. Surgery to alter the clavicle is a separate topic with its own risks, covered in the clavicle lengthening osteotomy article.

lead: Biacromial width, the span across the acromion processes of the shoulder blades, and clavicle length are discussed in looksmaxxing as the bone-set limits on shoulder width. Members commonly say that training can add muscle on the outside of this frame but cannot change the skeleton [1].

Wikipedia describes the clavicle as an S-shaped long bone lying horizontally between shoulder blade and sternum. It reports that males usually have longer and larger clavicles than females, and that the bone begins ossifying very early in fetal life but finishes only around age 21 to 25 [2].
No clinical studies of biacromial or clavicle width as an attractiveness or looksmaxxing target were found.
infobox: Not the bone; muscle adds soft-tissue width

paras: The clavicle acts as a strut that holds the shoulder away from the trunk. It has a medial sternal end, a lateral acromial end and a shaft. In one study of 748 males and 252 females, cited on Wikipedia, clavicle length grew by roughly 5 to 6 mm between the 18 to 20 and 21 to 25 age groups [2].
The deltoid arises partly from the clavicle and acromion, so soft tissue contributes to total shoulder width beyond the bone [3].

A looksmax.org thread asks what a good clavicle width and bideltoid size are. The poster, 5 feet 6 inches tall, reports an 18 inch clavicle width and 20 inch bideltoid width and says the frame still looks narrow to them, and replies trade figures and targets [1]. The thread notes that the average bideltoid width is not well documented and that clavicle width data are hard to find.
Members use these metrics to decide how much of their shoulder appearance can be changed by training and how much is skeletal.

Anthropometric research measures shoulder breadth in various populations, but the sources reviewed do not include norms for biacromial width in the forum sense, nor studies linking it to attractiveness. Clinical literature on the clavicle focuses largely on fractures and their surgical management [4].
No studies found on biacromial or clavicle width as an appearance target.

lore.intro: Clavicle and bideltoid numbers are posted for comparison, with some users setting large target figures for the frame [1].

claims.claim: Clavicle width sets the ceiling for how wide the shoulders can look.
claims.believers: Users say the bone is the part they cannot train and that it drives the 'twink' versus broad impression [1].
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes the clavicle's length differs by sex and finishes growing in the early twenties [2]. No study tested its role in perceived attractiveness.

claims.claim: Specific bideltoid numbers (for example 24 inches) define a high-status frame.
claims.believers: Some posters name large figures as targets [1].
claims.experts: No population norms or attractiveness thresholds for such figures were found in published sources.
